RE: LD 779- An Act to Fund the Aroostook County Drug Treatment Court

Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Distinguished Members of the Judiciary Committee:
My name is Elizabeth Simoni. I am writing to you today in support of LD 779, An Act to Fund the
Aroostook County Drug Treatment Court. I serve as the executive director of Maine Pretrial Services, Inc. (MPS), a private non-profit organization which provides services in thirteen Maine counties. In addition
to pretrial screening, pretrial release, community supervision, and case management, MPS also provides
case management for each of Maine's treatment recovery courts, including the existing adult criminal
courts, the veterans treatment courts, the co-occurring disorders court, and the family recovery courts.
MPS has provided services to Maine's drug courts since the first Maine Treatment Court was formed in Cumberland County in 1996. I was fortunate to be in my current role at that time and have been deeply
committed to these courts ever since.

Currently, Aroostook County is the only Maine county that does not have at least one treatment recovery
court. An Aroostook County Treatment Recovery Court was recommended in an independent, formal
evaluation of Maine's adult criminal treatment courts (Recommendation 2, Executive Summary, Public Consulting Group, December 2019). At that time, there were two prosecutorial districts in Maine without treatment recovery courts. Given the demonstrated efficacy of treatment courts in reducing criminal recidivism and assisting individuals with lengthy criminal histories with acute needs for substance use and mental health treatment, having a treatment court in each district is not only equitable, it is best practice in a continuum of solution driven justice interventions.
The system of treatment courts in Maine is well established and the infrastructure exists to add another court. Statewide practice, if replicated in Aroostook County, will assure adherence to the national best practice standards for treatment courts, as promulgated by All Rise (formerly the National Association of Treatment Court Professionals). Treatment Courts, when adherent to national best practice standards, assure reductions in recidivism that far surpass those measured in traditional case processing.
Treatment Courts remain the most researched criminal legal therapeutic intervention globally, and are clear standard bearers for evidence based, research driven practices. As part of its role in Maine's
treatment recovery courts, MPS is responsible for capturing all pertinent data points regarding referrals,
admissions, case progress, completions, terminations, and more. If a treatment court is opened in
Aroostook, MPS will assure regular, thorough data collection to aid in outcome measurement and
evaluation.

Reductions in criminal recidivism, improved quality of life, and enhancements to public safety are all hall marks of a high functioning treatment recovery court. The benefits also include demonstrated cost reductions as compared to jail and prison sentences served as results of traditional criminal case
processing. In short, treatment courts make good sense for individuals, communities, and criminal legal
systems.
If funded, an Aroostook Couit will benefit from the deep experience of treatment court practitioners from other Maine jurisdictions, while honoring and uplifting the wisdom and experiences unique to Aroostook County practitioners. The recent multi-disciplinary and highly collaborative efforts of the Aroostook County treatment court planning group chaired by Aroostook County District Attorney Todd Collins and Specialty Dockets and Grants Coordinator Todd Crawford exemplified this strength. Thank you for your dedication to the State of Maine and thank you for your serious consideration of this important bill.
Respectfully Submitted,
Elizabeth Simoni Executive Director Maine Pretrial Services, Inc.

LD 779: An Act to Fund the Aroostook County Drug Treatment Court
Presented to Maine's Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary
As the state's largest grassroots mental health advocacy organization, NAMI Maine supports the passage of LD 753: An Act to Support an Aroostook Adult Treatment and Recovery Court. As an organization representing one in four Mainers diagnosed with a mental health condition each year and their families, and as the sole provider implementing Platinum Level Certified Crisis Intervention Teams across the state, we commend initiatives that support the diversion of individuals from the criminal justice system and support the treatment and recovery of our friends and neighbors.
NAMI Maine collected data regarding 315 mental health calls responded to by law enforcement in Aroostook County. One hundred and eighty-three of those individuals interacted with law enforcement on multiple occasions due to their behavioral health challenges, with 73 of those individuals interacting with law enforcement more than ten times in the previous six months. Of those calls, 49 individuals were arrested by law enforcement, with anecdotal statements from law enforcement reflecting that, at times, this was the only avenue they saw available to access treatment for the individual.
Research has indicated that Treatment Courts are a cost-effective practice to support individuals who are struggling with behavioral health challenges in communities, resulting in the intersection with the criminal justice system. Treatment courts have found that for every $1 spent in this model, taxpayers average $2-$4 in savings, with some communities reporting as high as $26. Long-term impacts of treatment courts demonstrate a significant reduction in recidivism rates for those who graduate from the program. For those who do experience recidivism, there is a minimal risk of escalation of crimes, which is correlated with employment rates, stable housing, and consistent case management services.1
Maine is currently in a tenuous position regarding the behavioral health challenges facing our state, which has limited resources and services while also addressing fiscal challenges. Treatment courts are demonstrated to be cost-effective alternatives to incarceration, providing treatment and services while diverting from the higher and more costly levels of care of incarceration. Additionally, when implemented with fidelity, treatment courts assist individuals with building natural and sustainable support networks, resulting in higher success rates in long-term stability within the community setting. Because of this, NAMI Maine supports LD 753 and the work to provide recognized alternatives to incarceration and services to Aroostook County.

ABOUT NAMI MAINE: Incorporated in 1984, the National Alliance on Mental Illness, Maine Chapter (NAMI Maine) is the state's largest grassroots mental health organization. With support from national and regional affiliates, the agency is dedicated to building better lives for everyone impacted by behavioral health concerns. NAMI Maine engages with leaders and community partners at all levels to improve the state's mental health system through collaboration and education.

Re: LD 753 - An Act to Support an Aroostook Adult Treatment and Recovery Court and LD 779 An Act to Fund the Aroostook County Drug Treatment Court

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide information as you consider LD 753 - An Act to Support an Aroostook Adult Treatment and Recovery Court and LD 779 An Act to Fund the Aroostook County Drug Treatment Court.

An Adult Treatment and Recovery Court in Aroostook County would align the state's most rural region with most other counties in Maine and nine (9) existing Treatment and Recovery Courts. These courts, or rather the case management and treatment services offered through the court process, offer individuals a pathway to treatment and recovery rather than incarceration through contracts with Maine Pretrial Services. As written, both of these bills provide funding to establish and maintain such courts. LD 753 provides ongoing funding in the amount of $1 million to the Judicial Branch's General Fund in both FY 2025-26 and 2026-26, while LD 779 intends to utilize $179,500 from the Opioid Use Prevention and Treatment Fund and provide the Office of Behavioral Health (OBH) with $561,283 in one-time funding to contract for the pretrial services for this court.

However, as proposed, LD 753 does not identify any funding for the critical behavioral health treatment and case management services required by these courts; it identifies funding only for the establishment and operations of the court itself. If the Committee chooses to move forward with this legislation, it is critical that an additional $500,180 in ongoing funding is provided to OBH to ensure the behavioral health services, training, incentives, and other ancillary responsibilities associated with the case management and treatment services, as well as staffing for two Peer Recovery positions, which are foundational components of Treatment and Recovery Courts, are fully funded.

While LD 779 does contemplate funding to OBH at an appropriate level, the funding is only onetime and is taken from the Opioid Use Prevention and Treatment Fund (OPTF), which is already fully obligated for other opioid response initiatives, including those that support prevention and children, youth and families. Any additional funding obligations in the OPTF would require

eliminating or discontinuing current initiatives. As such, we oppose the use of OPTF to cover these funding needs.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Sarah Squirrell Director Office of Behavioral Health Maine Department of Health and Human Services

RE: Public Hearing on LD753 and LD 779

SUBMITTED VIA EMAIL

Good day Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee.
Thank you for this opportunity to present written testimony on the proposed legislation affecting Maine's criminal laws and access to criminal justice before you today. I am offering this testimony individually as the District Attorney for Aroostook County and not on behalf of any organization or other prosecutorial district.
I write in support of LD 753 and LD 779. While we know that these Bills seeking to facilitate an Adult Treatment and Recovery Court (ATRC) in Aroostook County is not a "silver bullet" or a complete answer to serious substance abuse problems in our communities; LDs 753 and 779, never-the-less, can be a significant part of the solution.
While the ultimate causes of drug abuse and addiction are as varied and individual as those caught in its powerful grasp, the effects of drug and substance abuse are too well known to the law enforcement community and the friends, neighbors, and families of the abuser. Those effects are concrete, widespread, and often tragic.
Within the last several years, even in an often idyllic and rural County like Aroostook, we have lost too many people to the dire consequences of drug abuse - some have been hospitalized or have died from selfpoisoning by overdose; some have been injured, maimed, or have died at the hands of an intoxicated substance abuser operating a motor vehicle or ATV; some have succumbed to the years of abuse and expired years before their natural time; others, compelled by a seemingly insatiable hunger and desire for drugs, have preyed upon their communities committing thefts, ranging from the petty - by pilfering money, property, and prescription medications from family and friends - to the absolutely destructive - by invading people's homes and stealing money and property, or by raiding medicine cabinets, or by stripping buildings of copper wire and plumbing; by assaulting or robbing others, often to either acquire more drugs

or to settle some sort of drug debt, real or imagined; others resort to selling the very poison of their own addiction and spread their affliction to an ever-growing supply of new customers.
Our tools in responding to the drug problem are rough - jail and the threat of jail. Jail offers a deterrent, but only to those who will listen. Those who are not deterred often wait for a "bottom" before they seriously attempt to remove themselves from the influence of drugs and other drugged people. Far too often, that "bottom" comes at the expense of others - usually in the form of significant criminal activity. I do not see how we can, in good conscience wait for someone to kill, injure, maim, burglarize, rob, or steal before we step in and demand a "serious" response to a serious problem. These are only some of the more significant and serious consequences of drug and substance facilitated crime and not the equally destructive, painful, and far-too-often tragic social and economic effects of drug and substance abuse - like babies born drug-affected or other children caught in the crossfires of addiction.
We can seek to reduce the demand of drugs by limiting the number of people in Maine who start down the path of abuse and addiction by enacting tough laws to discourage those who will listen from being experimental and casual users of illicit substances. We can attempt to limit the supply of drugs into Maine by making it riskier to import, possess, and deliver those drugs within our borders. We need people to enforce those laws. Additionally, we can seek to give current users the tools they need to successfully leave the drugged life behind and to escape the heavy gravity that illicit drugs and the drug scene provides and create opportunities for a successful recovery process.
As my initial commentary would indicate, the criminal activity surrounding the abuse of illicit substances is not limited to drug trafficking and drug "crimes" alone. The scope of drug related crime expands into nearly every corner of the criminal justice system; from OUI enforcement to petty and grand thefts, to home invasions and burglaries, to crimes of violence and retribution, and even to fatal self-poisonings and drug-induced vehicular homicides.
LDs 753 and 779 focus on the creation of an ATRC in Aroostook County, which is both admirable and has the potential to significantly impact the lives of those Defendants in a positive and productive way. Ideally the creation of a Drug Court will have a positive impact across all facets of Aroostook County life. Increased education, increased access to treatment, and more treatment providers in the community are just some of those potential positive impacts.
The goal of any successful substance use program in the criminal justice system must balance the individual needs of a defendant without losing sight of the crime committed and the harm to the community that their conduct created. Accountability is an important facet of recovery. When we address the whole of the person, the good, the bad, and the in between then we can build bridges to successful reintegration with their community, even if those successes start small. As we gather small successes and build on them with the client, we will slowly exchange the external motivating factors of avoiding prison with internal, but concrete motivating ones like home, family, and work or education. Intervention will be a success when the client's reasons for not doing drugs or alcohol outweigh their desire to use. In other words, we want to mitigate a defendant's desperate desire to escape reality, not just by force and fear, but by making their reality better.
The drug problem facing Maine and Aroostook County is multi-faceted and complicated; and it requires a broad, community-based solution. LDs 753 and 779 and the creation of a Treatment and Recovery Court in Aroostook County will be an integral part of that solution.
Be Well and Stay Safe,
Todd R. Collins District Attorney, Aroostook County
